objectives: Sequence the events of systole and diastole using the Wiggers diagram.
Compute cardiac output from heart rate and stroke volume and reason about the Frank-Starling mechanism.
Distinguish preload from afterload and relate them to ejection fraction and ventricular function curves.

slides.title: Systole, diastole, and the Wiggers diagram
slides.body:
The **cardiac cycle** is one complete heartbeat, divided into **systole** (contraction and ejection) and **diastole** (relaxation and filling). The canonical way to see all the simultaneous events is the **Wiggers diagram**, devised by the American physiologist **Carl Wiggers** (1883-1963), which stacks several traces against a common time axis: left-ventricular pressure, aortic pressure, left-atrial pressure, ventricular volume, the **electrocardiogram (ECG)**, and the **phonocardiogram** (heart sounds).

Reading the Wiggers diagram for the left heart, the sequence is:

- **Atrial systole.** The ECG **P wave** triggers atrial contraction, topping off ventricular filling with the 'atrial kick' (~10-20% of filling) and producing the **a wave** in the atrial pressure trace. The ventricle is now at **end-diastolic volume**.
- **Isovolumetric contraction.** The **QRS complex** triggers ventricular contraction; pressure shoots up, the **mitral valve** slams shut producing the first heart sound **S1**, and with both valves closed volume is constant.
- **Rapid then reduced ejection.** When LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure (~80 mmHg) the **aortic valve** opens and blood is ejected; ventricular volume falls toward **end-systolic volume**. Aortic pressure peaks at the **systolic pressure** (~120 mmHg).
- **Isovolumetric relaxation.** The **T wave** marks repolarization; the ventricle relaxes, pressure falls, the aortic valve closes producing the second heart sound **S2** and the **dicrotic notch** (a small upward blip) in the aortic trace. Both valves are again shut.
- **Rapid then reduced filling.** When LV pressure drops below atrial pressure the **mitral valve** opens and the ventricle fills passively, refilling to end-diastolic volume.

Several landmarks deserve memorizing. The **dicrotic notch** marks aortic-valve closure and the onset of diastole. The atrial pressure trace shows three positive waves — the **a wave** (atrial contraction), the **c wave** (tricuspid/mitral bulging during isovolumetric contraction), and the **v wave** (atrial filling against a closed AV valve). A third heart sound **S3**, if present, occurs in early rapid filling and can signal a dilated, failing ventricle; a fourth sound **S4** occurs with atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle. Crucially, **diastole is longer than systole** at rest (roughly two-thirds versus one-third of the cycle), and because coronary flow occurs mainly in diastole, anything that shortens diastole — tachycardia, for example — disproportionately reduces coronary perfusion. The entire diagram repeats every cardiac cycle, and its internal timing is set by the conduction system you have already studied.

slides.title: Cardiac output and the Frank-Starling mechanism
slides.body:
The headline number of cardiac performance is **cardiac output (CO)** — the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute. It is the product of how often the heart beats and how much it ejects each beat:

$$CO = HR \times SV$$

where $HR$ is heart rate (beats/min) and $SV$ is stroke volume (mL/beat). For a resting adult at $HR = 70$ bpm and $SV = 70$ mL, $CO = 70 \times 70 = 4900$ mL/min $\approx 5$ L/min — roughly the entire blood volume circulated each minute. During heavy exercise, $CO$ can rise to **20-25 L/min** in athletes through increases in both heart rate and stroke volume. To compare people of different sizes, clinicians normalize to body surface area as the **cardiac index** $CI = CO / BSA$, normally about 2.5-4.0 L/min/m$^2$.

Stroke volume itself depends on three factors — **preload, afterload, and contractility** — but the most elegant is preload, governed by the **Frank-Starling mechanism**. Named for **Otto Frank** (frog-heart studies, 1895) and **Ernest Starling** (dog heart-lung preparation, 1918), the law states: *the greater the volume of blood filling the heart in diastole (the preload), the greater the force of contraction and the larger the stroke volume*, within physiological limits. Plotting stroke volume (or stroke work) against end-diastolic volume produces the **ventricular function curve** (the Starling curve), which rises steeply then plateaus.

The molecular basis lies in the **sarcomere**. As the myocardium is stretched by greater filling, the overlap between **actin** and **myosin** filaments approaches optimal, and — more importantly in cardiac muscle — stretch increases the **calcium sensitivity** of the contractile proteins (a length-dependent activation involving **titin** and **troponin C**). So a more-filled ventricle contracts harder, automatically matching output to venous return. This is why the right and left ventricles, pumping in series, stay balanced: if venous return to the right heart rises, the right ventricle ejects more, which raises filling of the left heart, which then ejects more in turn.

The Frank-Starling mechanism also explains compensation and failure. Acutely, a failing heart climbs its (depressed) Starling curve by retaining fluid to raise preload, maintaining output at the cost of congestion. But a chronically overstretched, failing ventricle operates on a flat or descending curve, where further filling only raises pressures (causing pulmonary edema) without raising output — the rationale for **diuretics** in heart failure, which lower preload and move the patient leftward off the congested portion of the curve.

slides.title: Preload, afterload, and ejection fraction in practice
slides.body:
Two loads bracket every contraction, and confusing them leads to wrong clinical decisions. **Preload** is the ventricular stretch at the *end of filling*, indexed by **end-diastolic volume** or by filling pressures such as **central venous pressure** (right heart) and **pulmonary capillary wedge pressure** (left heart, measured with a **Swan-Ganz catheter**, introduced by Jeremy Swan and William Ganz in 1970). Preload rises with increased blood volume, increased venous return, and a long diastole; it falls with hemorrhage, dehydration, and venodilators such as **nitroglycerin**.

**Afterload** is the resistance the ventricle pumps *against* during ejection — for the left ventricle, chiefly the **systemic vascular resistance (SVR)** and aortic impedance; for the right ventricle, the **pulmonary vascular resistance**. The ventricular wall stress is described by the **law of Laplace**, $\sigma = \frac{P \cdot r}{2h}$: a hypertensive patient with high aortic pressure $P$, or a dilated ventricle with large radius $r$, faces higher wall stress, raising the heart's oxygen demand. Afterload rises with hypertension, **aortic stenosis**, and vasoconstriction; it falls with **arterial vasodilators** such as ACE inhibitors and hydralazine.

The interplay is captured by two effects of afterload on the pressure-volume loop. Raising afterload (higher arterial pressure) means the aortic valve opens at a higher pressure, the ventricle ejects less before end-systole, so **end-systolic volume rises and stroke volume falls** — for a given contractility. Conversely, reducing afterload (vasodilation) lets the ventricle empty more, raising stroke volume, which is the central reason **afterload reduction** improves output in heart failure.

**Ejection fraction (EF)** unites these into the everyday clinical index:

$$EF = \frac{SV}{EDV} \times 100\% = \frac{EDV - ESV}{EDV} \times 100\%$$

Measured by **echocardiography**, cardiac MRI, or contrast ventriculography, a normal LV EF is **55-70%**. EF separates the two major phenotypes of heart failure: **HFrEF** (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, EF below ~40%, a problem of contraction) and **HFpEF** (preserved ejection fraction, EF above ~50%, a problem of stiff ventricular filling). A worked example fixes the ideas: a ventricle with $EDV = 150$ mL and $ESV = 90$ mL has $SV = 60$ mL and $EF = 60/150 = 40\%$ — borderline, suggesting early systolic dysfunction. The same ventricle given an afterload-reducing drug might empty to $ESV = 70$ mL, raising $SV$ to 80 mL and $EF$ to 53% without any change in filling. Reading these numbers correctly, in the context of preload and afterload, is the daily work of the cardiologist.

question.question: A patient has a heart rate of 80 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 65 mL. Compute the cardiac output in liters per minute, rounded to one decimal place.
question.hint: CO = HR x SV. Multiply 80 by 65 to get mL/min, then divide by 1000 for L/min.

question.question: On the Wiggers diagram, the dicrotic notch in the aortic pressure trace marks which event?
options: Opening of the mitral valve at the start of filling
Closure of the aortic valve at the start of diastole
Atrial contraction producing the a wave
Opening of the aortic valve at the start of ejection
question.explanation: The dicrotic notch (incisura) is the brief upward deflection in the aortic pressure trace caused by aortic valve closure and the elastic recoil of the aorta at the onset of diastole. It coincides with the second heart sound S2. Mitral opening and atrial contraction are atrial-side events; aortic valve opening begins ejection without producing the notch.

hints: The notch appears at the very end of ejection.
It coincides with the second heart sound, S2.
slides.workedSolution: The dicrotic notch reflects aortic-valve closure and aortic recoil at the start of diastole, coinciding with S2. It cleanly separates systolic ejection from diastolic filling on the aortic trace.

question.question: Holding contractility and preload constant, a sudden rise in afterload (arterial pressure) will:
options: Increase stroke volume and decrease end-systolic volume
Decrease stroke volume and increase end-systolic volume
Leave stroke volume and end-systolic volume unchanged
Increase both stroke volume and end-diastolic volume
question.explanation: Higher afterload means the aortic valve opens at a higher pressure and the ventricle cannot eject as far before end-systole, so end-systolic volume rises and stroke volume (EDV minus ESV) falls — for a fixed contractility and preload. This is why afterload reduction helps the failing heart eject more.

hints: Think about how far the ventricle can empty against a higher pressure.
If the ventricle ejects less, what happens to the leftover (end-systolic) volume?
slides.workedSolution: Increased afterload raises the pressure at which the aortic valve opens, so ejection stops earlier; ESV rises and SV falls. Reducing afterload reverses this, the basis of vasodilator therapy in HFrEF.

question.question: A failing heart on the Starling curve
question.prompt: A patient with chronic heart failure arrives short of breath with swollen legs and crackles in both lungs, indicating fluid overload, yet a low cardiac output. Using the Frank-Starling ventricular function curve, explain why this patient is operating on the flat (plateau) portion of a depressed curve, why simply giving more intravenous fluid would worsen the pulmonary congestion without improving output, and how a diuretic plus an afterload-reducing agent would move the patient to a better operating point. Reference preload, afterload, and the shape of the Starling curve in your reasoning.

question.question: A ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 160 mL and ejects a stroke volume of 64 mL. Compute the ejection fraction as a percentage.
question.hint: EF = SV / EDV * 100%. Divide 64 by 160 and multiply by 100.
